nameStory: This tiny aquatic organism gets its scientific name from Greek words meaning 'false little disk' - though it's not actually disk-shaped at all! The 'cornutum' part means 'horned,' referring to the little horn-like projections that stick out from each cell, making it look like a microscopic star with pointed tips.
description: Pseudopediastrum cornutum is a microscopic green alga that lives in freshwater ponds and lakes throughout New England. Each individual is actually a beautiful star-shaped colony of 4-16 cells arranged in a flat, circular pattern, typically measuring just 20-50 micrometers across - far too small to see without a microscope. The cells are connected at their centers, with each cell extending outward like the points of a star, creating an intricate geometric pattern that looks almost like nature's own snowflake. You'll need a microscope and a sample of pond water to observe these tiny living jewels.

idTips.label: Star-shaped colony
idTips.description: Flat, circular arrangement of 4-16 cells radiating outward from a central point, creating a distinctive star or wheel-like pattern when viewed under a microscope

idTips.label: Horn-like projections
idTips.description: Each cell has 1-2 pointed horn-like extensions (processes) that stick out beyond the colony's edge, giving it a spiky appearance

idTips.label: Connected cell centers
idTips.description: All cells in the colony are joined together at their inner ends, creating a solid central connection point

idTips.label: Bright green color
idTips.description: Vibrant green coloration from chlorophyll, easily distinguished from colorless or brownish microscopic organisms in the same water sample

idTips.label: Single layer arrangement
idTips.description: All cells lie in one flat plane - never stacked on top of each other - creating a two-dimensional geometric pattern

habitat: Found in the shallow, warmer waters of ponds, small lakes, and slow-moving streams throughout New England, particularly in areas with moderate nutrient levels. It thrives in the quiet backwaters and protected coves where organic matter has settled, often alongside other microscopic algae and aquatic plants like pondweeds and water lilies.

seasonality.spring: Populations begin growing as water temperatures warm, often becoming more abundant in late spring samples from pond edges and shallow areas.
seasonality.summer: Peak abundance occurs during warm summer months when water temperatures and nutrient levels are optimal for growth and reproduction.
seasonality.fall: Still present but populations may decline as temperatures cool and daylight hours decrease, though colonies can persist into early fall.
seasonality.winter: Largely dormant or absent from water samples during freezing periods, surviving as resistant spores or stages until spring warming.

funFact: Despite being invisible to the naked eye, a single drop of pond water can contain hundreds of these geometric masterpieces, each one a perfectly symmetrical living mandala that reproduces by splitting apart and reforming into new star patterns!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with its close relative Pseudopediastrum boryanum, but cornutum has more pronounced horn-like projections and typically forms more angular, pointed star shapes, while boryanum tends to be more rounded with shorter or absent horns.
contextualKnowledge: This species was recently moved from the genus Pediastrum to Pseudopediastrum based on genetic studies, so you may find it listed under its old name in older field guides and references - it's the same organism, just with an updated scientific classification.
compareHints: Compared to Pseudopediastrum boryanum, cornutum has more prominent and longer horn-like projections extending from each cell, creating a more spiky, angular appearance. The overall colony shape is also more distinctly star-like rather than the smoother, more circular outline typical of boryanum. The cell arrangements tend to be more geometric and rigid-looking in cornutum.
